title: PosterAgent: Iterative Design via Agentic Reinforcement Learning
one_liner: A poster-making system learns to draft and then refine designs through trial and error, with different learning rules for each stage.
lead: Posters demand two competing skills: visual beauty and clear, readable text—neither of which text-to-image models handle well. This paper treats poster design as an agentic workflow: first draft a layout, then refine it step by step, guided by feedback. It uses a new learning method (Stage-Aware RL) that trains drafting and refinement as separate goals, because the two tasks require opposite skills: drafting needs risk-taking and exploration, while refinement needs precision and caution.

paras: Today's text-to-image models (systems that generate pictures from descriptions) can create beautiful images, but they cannot be edited afterward—if the text is unreadable or the layout is off-balance, you cannot fix it. They also consistently render text poorly: letters blur or distort.

Layout-generation methods (algorithms that arrange elements on a page) handle readable text and clear structure better than text-to-image models do, because they are designed to place text as separate objects instead of painting it. But they predict the entire design in one pass and stop. They have no loop to look at their own work and then make targeted improvements. This is a hard constraint because their architecture makes all decisions at once—they have no second chance, so if the initial prediction is imbalanced or unreadable, there is no way to improve it. A designer working on paper can sketch, judge, erase, and sketch again; these methods cannot.

callout.html: Current methods are either beautiful but unfixable, or editable but static. Neither learns to iterate.

panels.title: 1. The two old approaches
panels.viz_args: Text-to-image: pretty but broken. Layout: rigid, no fix.
panels.caption: Each tool does one job poorly and cannot learn or adapt.

panels.title: 2. Draft: the system sketches first
panels.caption: Agent places elements quickly; rough layout is deliberate, not final.

panels.title: 3. Feedback arrives: text readable? Balance good?
panels.viz_args: Score: 41/100. Feedback: text too small, layout lopsided.
panels.caption: The system reads its own work and learns what failed and why.

panels.title: 4. Refine: nudge text size, move boxes
panels.caption: Each adjustment targets the specific failures, guided by credit assignment.

panels.title: 5. Loop: the agent repeats until professional
panels.caption: Multiple refinement turns build a polished design from a rough start.

steps.b: Step 1: The agent drafts a full layout
steps.text: Starting from a brief and content list, generate an initial poster with text placement and element sizes.

steps.b: Step 2: Score the draft against design rubrics
steps.text: Measure readability, visual balance, and hierarchy; assign a score reflecting how close it is to professional.
From the score and design rules, identify which text is too small, which blocks clash, which layout principles were violated.
Adjust element sizes, reposition text and images, tweak spacing—each move targets a specific failure.
Loop steps 2–4 until the score plateaus or reaches a professional threshold.

object.h2: What the agent learns to move
paras: The agent controls two kinds of actions: placing and sizing elements during drafting (boxes, text height, images), and making small adjustments during refinement (nudging positions, changing font size, rebalancing padding). The trick is that these two action sets require different learning strategies: drafting rewards risk and exploration (try new layouts), while refinement rewards precision (fix one problem without breaking others).
object.object: design actions (layout positions and element sizes)

hidden.h2: Credit: which action fixed which mistake
hidden.name: credit assignment (which action caused which score improvement)
paras: Reinforcement learning works by trial and error: try a move, see if it improved the outcome, and if so, do it more often. To do that reliably, the system must link each move to the part of the outcome it caused—otherwise it cannot tell which moves are good and which are harmful. If it drafts a messy layout and then refines it twice, with scores going 40 to 80, the question arises: did the first refinement move do most of the work, or the second, or were both equally important? Without a clear answer, the system cannot learn which kinds of refinements actually work in the future because it is trying to learn from a blurry signal—the learning algorithm cannot tell whether the score improved because the draft was good (meaning refinement had easy work) or because the refinements were skillful (meaning they had to fix a bad draft). This matters because the system's next draft will be influenced by whichever action it thinks was responsible.

The paper introduces stage-aware credit assignment: instead of treating all actions as equivalent, it learns separate value functions (scoring rules) for drafting and refinement. A drafting action is judged by the question: 'did this initial move leave room for refinement to succeed later?' A refinement action is judged by: 'did this tweak fix a specific problem without breaking something else?' By splitting credit this way, each kind of action gets a clear signal: draft actions see whether their layout is refinable, and refinement actions see whether their fix actually worked. The learning becomes focused instead of confused because now each value function has a single, unambiguous signal to learn from.

heat.caption: Darker cells: actions with clear credit for improving the score. Highlighted: actions we strongly learned from.

reads.html: The hidden quantity is the answer to: 'which action was responsible for this improvement?' Learning a separate model for drafting vs. refinement makes this clear instead of ambiguous, because each model asks a different question: drafting models ask 'is this sketch refinable?' while refinement models ask 'did this fix work?'

Stage-Aware RL decouples value functions by phase: V_draft estimates the long-term value of a draft state, while V_refine estimates the value of making a refinement move. This works because drafting and refinement have different goals and answer to different signals, so separating the value functions prevents them from interfering with each other's learning.

paras: In standard reinforcement learning, the system sees a sequence of actions (draft, then refine, refine, refine) and a final score. It must assign credit backward: which action caused which part of the score? This is ambiguous when actions serve very different purposes.

The paper's insight: drafting and refinement are two distinct jobs. A good draft is not a beautiful design—it is a sketch that leaves room for refinement to work. A good refinement is a small targeted fix that improves one aspect without breaking others, because large changes risk cascading breakage and undo earlier fixes. These are opposite skills: drafting rewards exploration and openness, refinement rewards precision and caution. By learning two separate value functions (one asking 'is this draft refinable?' and one asking 'does this tweak improve things?'), the system avoids ambiguity because each value function sees a clear, single goal. Draft actions get signal on whether the layout is improvable; refinement actions get signal on whether each fix actually worked. This focused learning is faster and more reliable because the system is not trying to optimize two contradictory signals at once.

math.words: Loss for drafting actions plus loss for refinement actions. Drafting loss rewards states that leave room to improve. Refinement loss rewards moves that actually improve the score. Total loss is the weighted sum of both.
math.equation: L_total = lambda_d * L_draft + lambda_r * L_refine, where L_draft = (V_draft(s_t) - (gamma * V_draft(s_t+1) + r_draft_t))^2 and L_refine = (V_refine(s_t) - (gamma * V_refine(s_t+1) + r_refine_t))^2

how much improvement can a refinement move make from here
reward for drafting (potential for future improvement)
how much we value future score improvements versus immediate ones
weights balancing how much drafting and refinement matter in training

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Start: empty poster, V_draft = 0 (no structure yet).
Draft action: place text box and title. Reward is whether this draft looks refinable (e.g., text is placed but wrong size). V_draft goes to 50 (moderately refinable).
Refinement action 1: enlarge title text. Score jumps from 30 to 55. V_refine earns +25 reward for this move.
Refinement action 2: rebalance padding. Score jumps from 55 to 78. V_refine earns +23 reward.

Each stage's value function sees its own clear signal: drafting saw 'this setup is refinable' (V_draft improved), refinement saw 'this tweak worked' (score improved). No ambiguity about which action caused which gain.

math.note: Splitting the value function by stage means drafting is judged on setup potential, not final beauty, while refinement is judged on actual fixes—removing the confusion that arises when one training signal must cover both jobs.

charts.title: Standard RL (one value function)
charts.note: Single value function conflates drafting and refinement rewards. Unclear which actions matter for which goal. Learning is slow.

charts.title: Stage-Aware RL (this paper)
charts.note: Separate value functions for drafting and refinement. Each stage sees a clear credit signal. Learning is fast and precise.

items.html: If the learning heavily penalizes risky drafts, the agent learns to place everything in the safest, most boring arrangement, where refinement cannot do much. Stage-aware RL avoids this by rewarding draft-potential, not final score, but if tuned wrong it can still happen.

If refinement actions are tiny nudges (shift by 2 pixels, shrink by 1 point), the system cannot make deep fixes, so large improvements become impossible. Credit assignment might be correct, but the action space does not allow big-enough changes because the system cannot nudge far enough to change the core mistakes—if text is placed in the wrong area, moving it by 2 pixels will not fix it. The system learns precise movements but cannot fix core design mistakes.
The paper treats drafting and refinement as distinct. If the optimal strategy is to interleave small drafts with instant feedback, the two-stage separation may not discover that.

When stage-aware credit and a sufficiently varied action space are balanced, the system learns to sketch bold, explorable layouts and then execute precise, targeted fixes. Drafting learns to place elements in ways that give refinement room to work, and refinement learns which kinds of adjustments actually fix things.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a simple poster-design arena: given a random brief (headline, 3 bullet points, one image), the agent drafts a layout, scores it on three rubrics (text readable, elements balanced, hierarchy clear), then refines twice and shows the before-and-after. Train the agent on 100 random briefs using standard RL (one value function) and stage-aware RL (two value functions) in parallel. Measure: (1) average score after all refinement loops, (2) how much each stage contributes to quality improvement (draft refinability score plus refinement improvement score), (3) how many refinement loops before the score stops rising.
demo.metric_eq: final_score = baseline_score + sum_refine_i (score_i - score_i-1), where each refinement is a distinct contribution
demo.closing: The demo must show that stage-aware RL learns designs that are refinable (good draft setup) and actually improve under refinement (good adjustment skill), because separating the credit signal lets each stage specialize. Whereas single-value-function RL tends to learn either scared drafts (unrefined but safe, because exploration looks risky) or wasteful refinements (fine-tuning without foundation, because safe baseline looks better than risky setup).
